children: By Matt Grossman and Paul Vieira

ASHEVILLE, N.C.-Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney for the collapse of trade talks this month aimed at averting steep U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods, and brushed off concerns about a trade war with America's second-largest trading partner.

"I don't think you can be in a tit-for-tat [trade war] with someone who's 13 times larger than you are," Bessent said in an interview with CNBC Monday. "I think this is very unfortunate that Prime Minister Carney has turned this into a political shouting match," he added.

Bessent's comments were made on the sidelines of the G-20 finance ministers' conference, an annual gathering of economic officials from "the Group of 20" rich and developing countries aimed at promoting cooperation. Yet the breakdown of U.S.-Canada talks could be the start of a prolonged dispute, one of many driving allies apart and making international consensus more challenging than usual at this week's meetings.

Bessent said he plans to meet his Canadian counterpart, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, on the sidelines for further talks. In a statement Monday, Champagne said one of Canada's goals at the summit is to build more diverse global trading relationships-a priority for the Carney government because, Canadian officials say, the days of the U.S. as a reliable economic partner are over.

Bessent skipped last year's meeting in South Africa as Trump's trade war strained international relationships. This year, the U.S. is the host, and ministers from around the world are meeting at a sprawling resort in the Blue Ridge Mountains.

Bessent described America's turn to host the G-20 as an opportunity to get "back to the basics" and push for stronger global growth via deregulation. The setting in Asheville, in Western North Carolina, is also meant to showcase the region's recovery from a devastating hurricane two years ago.
This year's meeting has been overshadowed by a thorny set of global tensions once again centered on U.S. policy, and America's fraught relationships with allies and rivals alike.

This month, the U.S. placed tariffs on $20 billion of goods from Canada after dealmaking efforts fizzled. Canada intends to hit back with 50% tariffs on roughly 700 American products, from appliances to cheese, effective next Tuesday. The next round of U.S. retaliation-50% tariffs on Canadian-made vehicles and auto parts-is scheduled to hit Jan. 1, if the sides don't come to an agreement.

Meanwhile, the Iran conflict is threatening to drive a wedge between G-20 members after Bessent last week warned of sanctions on countries that assist Iran. China, Iran's largest trading partner, is part of the G-20. The war in Ukraine also pits a G-20 member, Russia, against Ukraine's Western allies. Bessent met with Russian finance minister Anton Siluanov in Asheville Monday.

Those tensions and others could make it harder than usual for the Asheville gathering to hammer out a statement of shared economic goals and commitments, the traditional product of these meetings, according to people familiar with the early rounds of talks.

Past G-20 finance ministers' meetings have reached consensus on issues such as cooperative trade and free currency markets-another topic that could be a sticking point after the U.S. sold euros to prop up the Japanese yen at Bessent's direction this summer.

Champagne told reporters in North Carolina that he is focused on encouraging Canadian economic data, most notably a solid 3.3% annualized jump in output in the April-to-June period, and the strongest quarterly growth in over three years. Partly fueling that growth, data shows, were increased exports to the U.S.
"We are just here to advocate for a level playing field," he told reporters, adding he has a good relationship with Bessent.

Later, a spokesman for Champagne said there is a scheduled bilateral meeting with the Treasury Secretary to advance Canada's trade interests. The spokesman's statement, sent via email, didn't directly address Bessent's criticism of Canada. Representatives for Prime Minister Carney didn't respond to a request for comment.

Over the weekend, Canada's chief negotiator on U.S. trade, Janice Charette, relayed her version of events leading to a collapse in trade negotiations. She said they contradicted what U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had disclosed in recent days.

"Our pens are down, but the door is open," Charette said in an interview with the Canadian Broadcasting Corp. "We're prepared to go and work with the United States on a deal that would be in the economic interest of Canadians, as long as it doesn't impact on Canadian sovereignty."

Two issues that led to a collapse in U.S.-Canada talks, Charette said, were 11th-hour demands to exclude medium- and heavy-duty trucks from tariff relief, and to give the U.S. a say over Canada's trading relations with other countries.
"We were not willing to accept a situation where the United States would dictate who we could do free trade agreements with," she said.
